milestones.title: King Helü of Wu founds his capital
milestones.detail: Later histories record that King Helü had his minister Wu Zixu lay out a walled capital, Helü City, in 514 BCE. Tradition identifies it with the old walled city of Suzhou.
milestones.source: Xu Yinong (2000), The Chinese City in Space and Time: The Development of Urban Form in Suzhou, University of Hawai'i Press, pp. 34-36, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzhou

milestones.title: Wu is conquered by Yue
milestones.detail: The state of Wu was defeated and annexed by Yue, ending the city's time as a royal capital. Yue was annexed in turn by Chu in 306 BCE.

milestones.title: The name Suzhou is first used
milestones.detail: Under the Sui dynasty the prefecture was officially named Suzhou, a contraction of the older name Gusu.

milestones.title: Grand Canal completed past the city
milestones.detail: Emperor Yang of Sui completed the Grand Canal network, whose Jiangnan section passes Suzhou and put the city on the main north-south trade route.
milestones.source: Ebrey, Cambridge Illustrated History of China, p. 114, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Canal_(China)

milestones.title: Pingjiang Tu city map carved in stone
milestones.detail: The stele map of Pingjiang (Suzhou) was engraved in 1229, the oldest surviving city plan in China. It shows the walled grid of streets and canals that the old town still follows.

milestones.title: Zhang Shicheng makes Suzhou his capital
milestones.detail: The rebel leader Zhang Shicheng seized Suzhou in 1356 and ruled his kingdom of Wu from the city.

milestones.title: City falls to Zhu Yuanzhang after a long siege
milestones.detail: Suzhou fell on 1 October 1367 after a ten-month siege. The future Ming founder then imposed heavy taxes on the city and prefecture.
milestones.source: Lorge (2005), War, Politics and Society in Early Modern China, pp. 101-105, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhang_Shicheng

milestones.title: Taiping forces capture Suzhou
milestones.detail: Taiping rebels took the prefectural city in 1860. Much of the city and many of its gardens were ruined during the occupation.

milestones.title: Qing and Ever-Victorious Army retake the city
milestones.detail: Li Hongzhang's Huai Army and Charles Gordon's Ever-Victorious Army recovered Suzhou at the end of 1863; the surrendered Taiping garrison was massacred.

milestones.title: Treaty of Shimonoseki opens Suzhou to trade
milestones.detail: Article 5 of the treaty that ended the First Sino-Japanese War opened Suzhou, with Hangzhou, Shashi and Chongqing, to foreign trade.

milestones.title: Railway to Shanghai opens
milestones.detail: Suzhou railway station opened on 16 July 1906 on the Shanghai-Nanjing line.

milestones.title: Japanese occupation
milestones.detail: Japanese forces invaded in 1937. Many gardens were again devastated by the end of the war.

milestones.title: Most of the city wall demolished
milestones.detail: The 15.2 km wall circuit was largely pulled down in 1958; about 2 km survives, including the Pan Gate.

milestones.title: Suzhou Industrial Park founded
milestones.detail: China and Singapore signed the agreement to develop Suzhou Industrial Park beside Jinji Lake on 26 February 1994, starting the city's eastward expansion.

milestones.title: Classical gardens inscribed by UNESCO
milestones.detail: The Classical Gardens of Suzhou were inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1997 and the listing was extended in 2000.

milestones.title: Metro Line 1 opens; Gusu District formed
milestones.detail: Suzhou Metro Line 1 began running on 28 April 2012. On 1 September the three old-town districts were merged into Gusu District.

landmarks.name: Tiger Hill Pagoda (Yunyan Temple Pagoda)
landmarks.note: Completion date from an inscribed casket found in 1957; the top storey was added in the Chongzhen reign (1628-1644).

landmarks.name: Twin Pagodas (Luohanyuan Shuangta)
landmarks.source: https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/罗汉院双塔 (height 33.3 m); http://www.china.org.cn/english/TR-e/43398.htm (built 982, 'more than thirty meters')

landmarks.name: Ruiguang Pagoda
landmarks.source: Chen Zehong (1999), Zhongguo guta zoubi, Guangdong People's Press, via https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/瑞光塔
landmarks.note: Height is given as 'about 43 m'. The brick body is dated 1009; the pagoda took its present seven-storey form in a rebuilding of 1119-1125, and other accounts date construction 1004-1030.

landmarks.name: Beisi Pagoda (North Temple Pagoda, Bao'en Temple)
landmarks.source: http://www.china.org.cn/english/TR-e/43399.htm (76 m, built 1131-1162); https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/报恩寺塔_(苏州市) (rebuilt 1153)
landmarks.note: English Wikipedia states that the Song pagoda burned and the present structure is a Ming rebuilding to the Song design; the completion year is therefore uncertain.

notes: Start date: 514 BCE is the traditional date, taken from later texts such as the Han-era Wu Yue Chunqiu, written centuries after the event, so it is marked 'estimated' rather than 'documented'. The date itself is not seriously disputed, but the site is: Chinese archaeologists variously place Helü's city at the Helü City site on the Wuxi-Changzhou border, at the Mudu ancient-city site in Suzhou's western suburbs (Zhang Weiming 2010), or under the present old town. The traditional view, followed here, is that the walled old town descends from it. Older legend puts the Wu state's origin with Taibo in the 11th century BCE at Wuxi; that is not used. Population: all pre-1950 points are Chandler's (1987) estimates as digitised by Reba, Reitsma & Seto (2016); we kept round-century values plus the 20th-century ones and dropped Chandler's intermediate years (810, 1080, 1102, 1150, 1184, 1250, 1350, 1371, 1378, 1393, 1450, 1491, 1522, 1550, 1575, 1650, 1657, 1735, 1810, 1825, 1830, 1863). There is no figure between 430 BCE and 800 CE, and no estimate at the founding date. Chandler's figures refer to the walled city and are low compared with other authorities: Modelski gives 100,000 for 400-300 BCE and for 700-1000 CE (120,000 in 600), the Encyclopaedia Britannica (11th ed., 1911, 'Su-chow', https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclopædia_Britannica/Su-chow) says the city was 'in 1907 credited still with a population of 500,000', and Wikipedia quotes the 1887 edition for a similar figure around 1880, and Wikipedia, citing Xu (2000) and Marme (2005), calls Suzhou the largest non-capital city in the world until about 1850, which implies a much larger population including the suburbs. No Chinese census figure before 1950 was located. Landmarks: Pan Gate (c. 1351), the Sanqing Hall of Xuanmiao Temple (1179), the Confucian Temple, Hanshan Temple, the Suzhou Museum and the Olympic Sports Centre were left out because no sourced height was found. Modern tower heights, years and coordinates are from the CTBUH Skyscraper Center city listing for Suzhou (coordinates checked against OpenStreetMap for Suzhou IFS; WGS-84). CTBUH gives 2015 for Gate to the East where Wikipedia gives 2016. Suzhou Zhongnan Center (planned 499 m) is on hold and is not included.
